clue.text: Decorate missing central point — that becomes showy (6)

indicators.note: something missing a part has lost it, so the word to decorate goes without one of its letters

blocks.note: to garnish a dish is to decorate it
N is a point of the compass, and it sits dead centre in the seven letters

explanation.surface: Someone decorating a room loses the focal point and the result tips into bad taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Central point' works twice over: N is a compass point, and it is also the middle letter of the word for decorate.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something loud, gaudy and over-bright is showy.

clue.text: Necktie Mike pinched from mum’s bed (5)

indicators.note: to pinch is to steal, and what is pinched from something is taken out of it

blocks.note: MA'S COT, a mother's bed, run together
Mike is M in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A tie called Mike has been nicked from mum's bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is reading 'mum's bed' as two words run together into one bigger word, which then loses its front letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Named after the Royal Ascot race meeting, this broad cravat is a kind of necktie.

clue.text: Planned in Hebridean island to accommodate wine lake (11)

indicators.note: to accommodate a guest is to put them up inside, so IN and the island take the wine inside them

blocks.note: tent is a deep-red Spanish wine

explanation.surface: Someone has planned something on a Scottish island involving a surplus of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wine lake' looks like the old EU surplus, but the two words part company: the wine goes inside, and the lake is a single map letter. This wine is an old crossword favourite worth knowing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something done on purpose was planned.

clue.text: Monopolise a crowd hosting ace winter celebration? (8)

indicators.note: a host has guests inside the house, so the crowd has the ace inside it

blocks.note: to hog is to keep to yourself
A = ace, as on playing cards

explanation.surface: Someone muscles in on a party crowd that has a star performer among it.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is one example of many: this is the Scottish New Year's Eve party, held on 31 December.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Scots' New Year's Eve festivity falls in midwinter.

clue.text: With this, evidence of engagement seen in desert? (7)

blocks.note: read the answer as three words: a ring worn on the finger
the verb: to leave someone in the lurch

explanation.surface: A wedding band worn on a hand gives someone away in the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as A BAND ON and it is an engagement ring being worn; 'With this' also nods to the phrase 'with abandon'. 'Desert' is the verb, not the Sahara.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb, leaving someone in the lurch; the second sense is the answer read as three words.

clue.text: Enjoy view in common area with endless grassy plot (5)

indicators.note: a word without an end has lost its last letter

blocks.note: a village lawn, with its final N cut off

explanation.surface: People share a view over a village common and its patch of grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Common' looks like the village green of the surface, but it belongs to the definition, and the grassy plot is the one that gets trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people who hold a view in common see eye to eye.

clue.text: Feature of bridge that needs care shown with maximum speed lowered (7)

indicators.note: something lowered is moved down, and in a down entry the C drops two places further down the word

blocks.note: a situation that needs care calls for this
c is the speed of light, the fastest there is: the letter C that moves

explanation.surface: A bridge warning notice about a lowered speed limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' is the card game, not a road over a river; the answer is its bidding round. Only one letter moves: the C slips down below the A and U.
explanation.definitionFit: In contract bridge the bidding phase before play carries this name, so it is a feature of the game.

clue.text: Shabby detective I went out with, necking drink (11)

indicators.note: to neck a drink is British slang for gulping it down, so the words swallow the drink

blocks.note: to lap is to drink like a cat
to date = to go out with someone

explanation.surface: A down-at-heel detective recalls a date who spent it gulping drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Necking' looks like kissing on a date, which fits the surface perfectly; here it is swallowing, and the drink goes between the detective and I.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a building or coat fallen into disrepair is shabby.

clue.text: Wanderer from Massachusetts bathed in green light (5)

indicators.note: something bathed in light is surrounded by it, so MA sits inside the green light

blocks.note: a nod is approval, a go-ahead
MA is the state's postal code

explanation.surface: A traveller from Boston stands bathed in a green glow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green light' reads as the colour of a lamp; it means permission, a sign of assent.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone with no fixed home, forever moving on, is a wanderer.

clue.text: Jazz fans head-to-head with very absorbing musical instruction (8)

indicators.note: two things head-to-head face each other with their fronts touching, so the first CAT is turned round until its C meets the other's C
to absorb is to soak up, so SO takes the pair inside it

blocks.note: cats are jazz fans; two of them, heads meeting

explanation.surface: Two jazz enthusiasts face off over how a passage should be played.
explanation.walkthrough: A cat is old slang for a jazz fan. 'Head-to-head' is a picture: two cats whose heads, the letter C, touch in the middle, so the left one reads backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A score marking telling the player to detach each note sharply is a musical instruction.

clue.text: Strong drink consumed by son and daughter hastily (9)

indicators.note: what is consumed is swallowed, so the drink ends up inside S and D

explanation.surface: Two children bolt down a stiff drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strong drink' reads as one phrase meaning spirits; 'Strong' is the definition on its own, and the drink is the mildest going.
explanation.definitionFit: Strong in the sense of firm in resolve and loyalty.

clue.text: Order to stop at sea a container with sulphur as cargo? (5)

indicators.note: cargo is carried in the hold, so the sulphur travels inside the container

blocks.note: A + VAT, the vat opening round its load
S is the chemical symbol for sulphur

explanation.surface: A ship is told to halt because it carries a drum of sulphur.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads like a naval order to stop a suspect cargo ship, which is fitting for a sailors' word.
explanation.definitionFit: The old nautical command to cease or hold fast is an order to stop at sea.

clue.text: At home, nothing is to stop French sweetheart showing decorative work (11)

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so the pieces fill the middle of the sweetheart

blocks.note: chérie = darling in French; it opens around the rest

explanation.surface: At home, someone refuses to let their French darling show off her craft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To stop' reads as refusing to allow; it means plugging, so three short pieces fill the sweetheart after her first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: European ornament imitating Chinese style is a kind of decorative work.

clue.text: Old journeymen — those against leaving Nag’s Head? (3,4)

indicators.note: a letter leaving a word walks out of it, so the N departs and is not in the answer

explanation.surface: A group of old workmen opposed to the pub, the Nag's Head.
explanation.walkthrough: The Nag's Head is a stock English pub name, but it only supplies one letter. The Wise Men journeyed to Bethlehem, so 'journeymen' is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wise Men who followed the star made the most famous ancient journey, so they are old journeymen.

clue.text: Particularly demanding aspect of ethics (11,10)

blocks.note: reads as 'especially tough'; really it glosses the two words: absolute, and commanding
reads as a vague part of moral life; really it names Kant's moral philosophy, where the principle sits

explanation.surface: A remark about the toughest part of moral philosophy.
explanation.walkthrough: Kant's unconditional moral command; the clue restates its two words in plain English, 'particularly' for the absolute first word and 'demanding' for the commanding second.
explanation.definitionFit: Kant's unconditional command is the central idea of his ethics.

clue.text: Cardinal put on clothes for early period (5,3)

indicators.note: a verb here: to clothe something is to wrap it, so STAGE wraps round the number

blocks.note: to stage a play is to put it on

explanation.surface: A cardinal dresses up in costume for an early service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal' paints a churchman and 'put on clothes' getting dressed; really it is a counting number, and 'clothes' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The earliest era of human prehistory, before metal tools, is an early period.

clue.text: Politician in India two journalists obstructed (7)

blocks.note: I is India in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A politician in India is hampered by a pair of reporters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Politician in India' means the politician placed after India's letter, not an Indian politician.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: hindered or blocked.

clue.text: Slogger run out — Jack intercepting whack (6)

indicators.note: to intercept is to cut in on something's path, so R, O and J cut into the middle of TAN

blocks.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
J = jack, as on playing cards

explanation.surface: A cricket scene: a big hitter is run out as the jack interrupts his shot.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on cricket, where a slogger hits hard and can be run out. Here a slogger is someone who slogs away at hard work.
explanation.definitionFit: From 'work like a Trojan': a tireless worker is a slogger.

clue.text: Endorsement given by diva in performing with alto (10)

indicators.note: letters that are performing are put through their paces, moving into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A star soprano sings alongside an alto and wins approval.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a concert review, and 'performing' fits it so naturally that it is easy to miss as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Official confirmation that something is sound amounts to an endorsement.

clue.text: Old man recalled element, allowed for inclusion for dessert (5,4)

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the old man comes back to front
something put in for inclusion goes inside, so LET is included within PART

explanation.surface: A father remembers a chemical element being allowed in a pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Element' suggests chemistry; it is simply a component, which opens up after its first letter to take in 'allowed'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a fruit pastry served after the main course is one dessert.

clue.text: Saint removed from evil church feature in fire (7)

indicators.note: a thing removed from somewhere is taken out of it, so the saint's S comes out of the evil

blocks.note: the tall pointed top of a church tower

explanation.surface: A saint is freed from wickedness in a church ablaze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' reads as flames in a church; it is the verb, to fire someone up.
explanation.definitionFit: To fill someone with enthusiasm is to fire them up.

clue.text: Maybe Stalin’s rule hit Castro badly, going into decline (12)

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, and botched letters come out in a mangled order
the jumbled letters go into the decline, which opens round them

blocks.note: a downturn; it splits after its first letter

explanation.surface: A comparison between two communist leaders as one regime falls into decay.
explanation.walkthrough: Stalin and Castro both belong to the picture, but only 'Maybe Stalin's rule' defines; Castro is just letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Stalin's absolute rule is the textbook case, hence 'Maybe'.

clue.text: Crate containing second part needed for pot (9)

indicators.note: a crate containing something holds it inside, so the S goes within the crate

explanation.surface: A packing crate holds a spare part for a cooking pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' sounds like a component to go in the crate; it is an actor's part, added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A lidded dish for slow oven cooking is a kind of pot.

clue.text: Science set down in working model (8)

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the record goes inside the model

blocks.note: to log is to write down

explanation.surface: A scientific theory is written up inside a working model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working model' is a single idea in the surface; in the wordplay the two words give two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The study of being, a branch of philosophy, counts as a science in the old broad sense of a body of knowledge.

clue.text: Society backed squeeze in political manipulation (4)

indicators.note: something backed is sent backwards, so the squeeze is turned back to front

blocks.note: a nip is a pinch or squeeze

explanation.surface: A society supports a squeeze as part of its political scheming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' reads as supported, which suits a political society; it means reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: The slanted presentation of news by party aides is political manipulation.

clue.text: Material possibly dangerous when used by top map-makers (8)

blocks.note: to top someone is to best them
the Ordnance Survey, Britain's national mapping agency

explanation.surface: A hazardous substance still in use by leading cartographers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top map-makers' reads as the best cartographers, but 'top' is a verb and the map-makers are Britain's official mapping body.
explanation.definitionFit: A fibrous mineral once used for fireproofing, harmful when its fibres are breathed in.

clue.text: Trade and oil supply interrupted by current leader (9)

indicators.note: read as supple-ly: something supple bends easily, so the letters bend into a new order
a thing interrupted has something cut into it, so the I is put into the fodder

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 'and' just joins the two words
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A market report: commerce and oil deliveries cut off by a power cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader' is the British term for a newspaper's lead opinion piece. 'Supply' is not the noun but the adverb of supple, the letters bending.
explanation.definitionFit: A British usage: a newspaper's leading opinion article is its leader.

clue.text: University to put in test for learning experience (8)

indicators.note: what is put in something goes inside it, so U and TO go into the test

explanation.surface: A university is put through an assessment as a teaching exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue belongs to the university world, so the answer sits naturally in the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A small teaching session with a tutor is a learning experience.

clue.text: Write number appearing within a small range (9)

indicators.note: something appearing within another shows up inside it, so the pen and the number sit inside A and S

blocks.note: A + S, S = small; it opens round the rest

explanation.surface: An instruction to write a number within a narrow band of values.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' looks like a span of numbers, the maths sense the surface sets up; it is a mountain range running down Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the mountains forming Italy's spine are a range.

clue.text: East German Oscar frames a Turner, that’s continuously repeated (8)

indicators.note: a frame goes round a picture, so the German east and the O go round the Turner

blocks.note: O is Oscar in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: An East German film award goes to a Turner painting that is shown over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A Turner' suggests the painter J.M.W. Turner, especially beside an Oscar; the Turner wanted is the singer.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical figure played over and over through a piece is something continuously repeated.

clue.text: Caste inside worshipped as god no longer restricted (12)

indicators.note: one thing inside another sits within it, so the caste goes within the word for worshipped as god

blocks.note: made a god of; it opens after its second letter
a caste is a social rank

explanation.surface: A caste once revered as divine loses its privileges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Restricted' seems to continue the story of a caste losing privilege; it is the secrecy of documents.
explanation.definitionFit: Documents released from secret status are no longer restricted.

clue.text: Encouraged war reporter encircling ancient hideout one duke’s abandoned (10)

indicators.note: to encircle is to go all round, so the war reporter goes round the rest
something abandoned is left behind, so one D is left out of the hideout

blocks.note: a journalist attached to a military unit
D = duke; only one of the two Ds goes

explanation.surface: A war correspondent surrounds an old hiding place that a duke has deserted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ancient hideout' has two Ds side by side, and 'one duke' is exact: dropping one leaves a word that itself means ancient.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: given courage, made bolder.

clue.text: Cobblers pursue proctor’s attendant (7)

blocks.note: cobblers and bull are both British slang for nonsense
to dog someone is to follow them

explanation.surface: Shoemakers chase after a university official's assistant.
explanation.walkthrough: At Oxford and Cambridge a proctor enforces discipline, helped by officers with a canine nickname. 'Cobblers' means rubbish, not shoemakers.
explanation.definitionFit: A university slang term: the officers who assist an Oxbridge proctor carry this nickname.

clue.text: Excellent emperor on vehicle carrying British cop to Chileans (10)

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another comes after it
to carry is to hold, so the excellent AI holds the B inside it

blocks.note: A1, first-rate, written with I for 1

explanation.surface: A fine emperor rides in a car with a British policeman to South America.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 appears as AI, the digit read as a letter, and it wraps round the B.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish regional word: a member of Chile's national police force.

clue.text: Employed as trainee, secretary sent back pennies — living cost frozen? (11)

indicators.note: something sent back returns the way it came, so the secretary reads backwards

blocks.note: the cost of somewhere to live

explanation.surface: A trainee's pay is sent back by the secretary while their living costs are frozen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frozen' reads as a price freeze on living costs; it is simply chilled, a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone bound to a master to learn a trade is employed as a trainee.

clue.text: Showing cheek perhaps accepting easy extra work (12)

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so the cheeky display takes 'easy' inside

blocks.note: baring your buttocks, your cheeks; it splits after its fourth letter

explanation.surface: A cheeky worker takes on a cushy second job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Showing cheek' reads as insolence; here the cheeks are the buttocks, and 'perhaps' flags the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing a second job on the side, often at night, is extra work.

clue.text: Make whole new lesson about overture to Hebrides — that was his (11)

indicators.note: a lesson made new is recast, so its letters are rearranged
about means around, so the rearranged letters go round the H

explanation.surface: A music lesson on the Hebrides overture, whose composer is the answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overture to Hebrides' is both a first letter and a real concert piece, so 'that was his' defines its composer.
explanation.definitionFit: The German composer wrote The Hebrides overture, also called Fingal's Cave, so it was his.

clue.text: Reference to ailment is revolting (11)

indicators.note: rebels in revolt rise up and overturn things, so the letters are overturned into a new order

explanation.surface: A mention of some illness is disgusting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' sits at the end like a comment on the illness; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A written statement vouching for someone's character is a reference.

clue.text: There’s deduction from pay with industrial action (8)

explanation.surface: Workers lose wages when they go on strike.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses sit in one realistic picture: strikers really do have money held back from their pay.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are British usage: a sum withheld from wages, and a strike halting work.

clue.text: English daisy for example good seasonal item (6,3)

explanation.surface: A spring flower offered as a good example of the season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daisy for example' reads as one phrase; the daisy gives a flower name and 'for example' stands alone as its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A chocolate treat sold only around one spring festival is a seasonal item.

clue.text: Suggestion from union freshly filled with purpose (8)

indicators.note: something done freshly is done anew, so the union is remade in a new order
a thing filled with something holds it inside, so the purpose goes inside the rearranged letters

explanation.surface: A trade union floats a new idea with real intent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' suggests a trade union, but it is only letters; 'purpose' is the aim, which sits near the end of the shuffled word.
explanation.definitionFit: An indirect hint, usually a sly or rude one, is a suggestion.

clue.text: Writer George in Silk Road city missing an old bit of Germany (4)

indicators.note: a city missing something has lost it, so the old coin is taken out of the city

blocks.note: the Uzbek city on the Silk Road
A + MARK, the old German currency

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old bit of Germany' sounds like a lost region; it is the Deutschmark, Germany's currency before the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: The French novelist Aurore Dupin wrote as George Sand.

clue.text: European resort — watercourse rising beneath it (8)

indicators.note: something rising goes upwards, and in a down entry that means reading from bottom to top
in a down entry, beneath means lower down, so the watercourse comes after the resort

explanation.surface: A European holiday resort with a stream coming up beneath it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a spring bubbling up under a spa; in the down grid that is literally the layout.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: someone from Spain is one European.

clue.text: French governess pressurised first person entering region round Metz (12)

indicators.note: someone entering a region goes into it, so the I goes inside the region

blocks.note: made someone do it = forced them
the French department whose capital is Metz

explanation.surface: A French governess is pressed into service in Lorraine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First person' tempts as the earliest arrival; it is the pronoun, which slips in after the region's second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An old English household usage: the French governess was addressed by this title.

clue.text: Dawn’s answer spoken after posh reader’s introduction (7)

indicators.note: in a down entry, something after comes later, so 'spoken' follows the posh reader
an introduction is what comes first, so only the first letter of reader is used

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dawn' reads as a woman's name; it is daybreak, and the possessive makes the definition an adjective. U is the old label for upper-class usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Named from Aurora, Roman goddess of daybreak, the adjective means belonging to the dawn.

clue.text: Zadok say: is he right, after disturbance, to seize power? (4,6)

indicators.note: letters that have been through a disturbance are thrown into disorder
to seize is to grab hold, so the jumbled letters grab the power inside them

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether Zadok was right to grab power after a coup.
explanation.walkthrough: Zadok anointed Solomon, and Handel's anthem 'Zadok the Priest' is sung at British coronations; 'say' marks him as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Zadok held the chief priestly office under David and Solomon.

clue.text: Amply bearded king in utility vehicle he owns? (7)

blocks.note: HIS UTE; a ute is a utility vehicle, a pickup

explanation.surface: A heavily bearded king sits in his pickup truck.
explanation.walkthrough: A ute is Australian slang for a utility vehicle, and 'he owns' makes it his; the king goes after the first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Hairy all over, as a thick beard is, so amply bearded.

clue.text: Unfortunate gag we’re told (6)

indicators.note: what we are told we hear rather than see, so the word is taken by its sound

explanation.surface: Someone unlucky is told to keep quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gag' tempts as a joke or a muzzle; it is heaving. 'Unfortunate' is a noun here, a pitiable person.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun sense: a luckless, miserable person is an unfortunate.

clue.text: Regularly harvested wheat in this Caribbean location (5)

indicators.note: letters harvested at regular intervals are picked every other one

explanation.surface: Wheat gathered at intervals in some island spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harvested' fits the wheat so well that it is easy to miss as part of the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the nation on western Hispaniola is a Caribbean location.

clue.text: Former Conservative employer’s apologist? (7)

blocks.note: one who employs something uses it

explanation.surface: A one-time Tory boss defends himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Employer' suggests a boss; here it is one who employs, puts to use, something. The 's is 'is'.

clue.text: God, canine, Anubis finally departing (5)

clue.text: Precisely locate cask in filling tankard (8)

clue.text: Smooth-shelled nut — tropical waterfowl dropping large one (5)

clue.text: Special occasion other than Anglican presumably? (5)

explanation.definitionFit: An old word for the present or particular occasion, now mostly in 'for the nonce'.

clue.text: Delivery usually associated with an address in southern England? (8,13)

clue.text: Clasp securing tot’s protective covering (8)

clue.text: Horse with info about duck being cooler underground? (7)

clue.text: Sorrow engulfing Miles seen before knight’s tomb (6)
